steps.claim: Two major earthquakes strike Mexico in September 2017

test.source: “Earthquakes and Crimes Against Women,” Feminist Economics, 2024

steps.note: The study covers two earthquakes that struck Mexico in September 2017. Dated here to the middle of that month.

steps.claim: Sexual abuse and rape rose after Mexico's earthquakes

test.design: official crime records in Mexico from before and after the earthquakes, against a comparison group
test.source: “Earthquakes and Crimes Against Women,” Feminist Economics, 2024
test.effect: After the earthquakes, sexual abuse rose by 11 percent and rape by 12 percent.
test.why: Quake damage disrupted schools, which probably pulled more students into gangs, and gangs played a big part in the extra abuse.
test.why_quote: gangs play an important role in the escalation of sexual abuse. Data on school damages further shows that disruptions to middle- and high-schools could have plausibly facilitated students’ gang membership

fx.quote: The article estimates causal effects using a difference-in-differences strategy and shows that following the earthquakes femicides decreased by 2 percent, sexual abuse rose by 11 percent, and rape climbed by 12 percent.

steps.note: From the paper: “The article estimates causal effects using a difference-in-differences strategy and shows that following the earthquakes femicides decreased by 2 percent, sexual abuse rose by 11 percent, and rape climbed by 12 percent.” The study uses official crime records from Mexico on crimes against women after two major earthquakes in September 2017.

steps.claim: The Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami hit Japan

test.source: “Natural Disasters and Political Participation: The Case of Japan and the 2011 Triple Disaster,” Journal of East Asian Studies, 2019

steps.note: The paper's abstract gives no study window, so the finding is dated to the stone.

steps.claim: More people took part in political groups in hard-hit regions

test.design: people in regions hit hard by the disaster against people in other regions, before and after
test.source: “Natural Disasters and Political Participation: The Case of Japan and the 2011 Triple Disaster,” Journal of East Asian Studies, 2019
test.effect: Taking part in political groups rose 6 percent in regions hit hard by the 2011 disaster.
test.why: Social ties carried the disaster's effect, since the rise in political activity came mostly from people with large social networks.
test.why_quote: the effect at the individual level is largely confined to individuals with large social networks

fx.quote: the 2011 triple disaster in Japan resulted in a 6 percent increase in participation in political groups in regions heavily affected by the disaster

steps.note: From the paper: “the 2011 triple disaster in Japan resulted in a 6 percent increase in participation in political groups in regions heavily affected by the disaster.” The study looks at the 2011 triple disaster in Japan, for both individual people and election districts.
